tier_reason: The c410-f3r blog compares aws-lc-rs, Graviola, ring and OpenSSL as swappable crypto backends of the wtx TLS stack; its code is public (wtx-bench.tar.xz: assets/bench.sh, src/main.rs, Cargo.toml profile 'deploy' opt-level=3/LTO/CGU1) and the CPU is stated (Ryzen 9 5900X), but no rustc or OpenSSL version is given, so it is not A. It is a personal blog by the wtx author (wtx 401 stars), not a well-known independent suite, so it is not B (same rule as quicperf and gonwan/webframework-benchmark).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page text: "OpenSSL is the slower library" and "Graviola is a promising new cryptography library". Numbers exist only as bar charts (hyperfine mean wall time per process, seconds, 0-0.010 s axis), not box plots. From the SVG bar heights (derived from page data): Graviola about 1.26-5.90 ms vs OpenSSL about 4.41-10.20 ms per full handshake process, about 1.6-3.8x; OpenSSL is slowest in all 45 combinations; Graviola is fastest in only 16 of 45 (ring or aws-lc-rs tie or win the rest).
corrections.workload: One process per run: decode 3 PEM files, then a full TLS 1.3 handshake over loopback TCP (server in main thread, client in another thread), then exit with no application data. wtx TLS stack with a swappable crypto backend (aws-lc-rs, Graviola, ring, OpenSSL via openssl-sys). 5 certificate signature algorithms x 3 key agreements (secp256r1, secp384r1, x25519) x 3 cipher suites. Timed with hyperfine -N, 10 runs after 10 warmups; mean plotted.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc version not stated (bench Cargo.toml: edition 2024, rust-version = 1.96, wtx 0.49 with 'nightly' feature); cargo profile 'deploy': opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, debug-assertions and overflow-checks off (from wtx-bench.tar.xz). OpenSSL version and build flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core, 32GB DDR4, Corsair Force MP510 SSD, Linux Fedora kernel 7.0.11-200.fc44.x86_64
corrections.caveats: Independent third-party blog by the wtx author, not a well-known suite; code is public in wtx-bench.tar.xz but rustc and OpenSSL versions are not stated. It times whole processes (startup, PEM decode, loopback TCP), and the OpenSSL-minus-Graviola gap is a near-constant 3.1-4.7 ms across all 45 combinations, which is consistent with a fixed per-process cost rather than faster handshake crypto; the author says the cause is unknown ("a missing compile flag, an internal misconfiguration, the openssl-sys crate or OpenSSL itself"). Graviola is fastest in only 16 of 45 combinations; ring matches or beats it on several, and aws-lc-rs beats it with ECDSA-P384 certificates. Numbers exist only in SVG bar charts (means of 10 runs). Graviola's own jbp.io/graviola page (Ryzen 9 7940HS, Apple M2, no compiler/flags) compares only against ring, aws-lc-rs, rustcrypto, golang, dalek and libcrux, not OpenSSL. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION; LICENSE and Cargo.toml give 'Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT-0' (the LICENSE prose says 'MIT license' but the included text is MIT-0).

notes: Real independent comparison against OpenSSL, but it comes from a small personal harness without compiler versions, and the OpenSSL gap looks like fixed process overhead, so the tier drops from B to C. The license is corrected from 'Apache-2.0 OR MIT OR ISC' to 'Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT-0'. Stars (305), last commit (2026-08-24) and active status check out.

tier_reason: The README Performance section says, word for word, that Fizz has 10% higher throughput than Meta's prior SSL library built on folly's AsyncSSLSocket (an OpenSSL libssl wrapper) and uses less memory per connection. This is a first-party number with no linked benchmark code, hardware, compiler, flags or data, so it is C.

corrections.caveats: First-party (Meta) README claim with no published methodology, hardware or reproducible artifact; the '10%' number is not backed by linked data. The sentence was added in commit 5a46d88 (2018-08-03) and has not changed since, so the baseline is Meta's 2018-era AsyncSSLSocket/OpenSSL stack; the exact OpenSSL version is not stated. Fizz itself still uses OpenSSL libcrypto and libsodium for crypto primitives (README Dependencies, fizz/CMakeLists.txt find_package(OpenSSL REQUIRED)), so the win is in the TLS 1.3 state machine and record layer (IOBuf scatter/gather, in-place encryption), not in faster crypto. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION; the LICENSE file is BSD 3-Clause text.

notes: The quote and the baseline match the README exactly, and the tier stays C. Metadata checks out: 1,202 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-26 (active), BSD-3-Clause per the LICENSE file. The only change is added caveat context: the 2018 date and the fact that Fizz still links OpenSSL libcrypto.
